The applicants were charged with membership of an illegal organisation under Article 314 of the Turkish Criminal Code (Law no. 5237).
On 1 April 2005 Law no. 5237 (the Turkish Criminal Code) entered into force.

At the material time, Article 220 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provided that anyone who establishes or directs an organisation for the purpose of criminal activity shall be liable to a term of imprisonment of between two and six years, provided that the structure of the organisation, the number of members and the quantity of equipment and supplies are sufficient to commit the intended crimes.

At the material time, Article 220 § 2 of the Turkish Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provided that anyone who becomes a member of an organisation established for the purpose of criminal activity shall be liable to a term of imprisonment of between one and three years.

At the material time, Article 220 § 3 of the Turkish Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provided that if the organisation is armed, the sentences stated in Article 220 §§ 1 and 2 shall be increased by between one quarter and one half.
At the material time, Article 220 § 4 of the Turkish Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provided that any crime committed within the framework of the organisation's activities shall be punished separately.

At the material time, Article 220 § 5 of the Turkish Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provided that the heads of a criminal organisation shall also be sentenced as perpetrators of all crimes committed within the framework of the organisation's activities.

At the material time, Article 220 § 6 of the Turkish Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provided that anyone who commits a crime on behalf of an illegal organisation, even if he is not a member of that organisation, shall also be punished for being a member of the organisation.

At the material time, Article 220 § 7 of the Turkish Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provided that anyone who aids an illegal organisation knowingly and willingly, even if he does not belong to the hierarchical structure of the organisation, shall be punished as a member of the organisation.

At the material time, Article 220 § 8 of the Turkish Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provided that anyone who spreads propaganda for the organisation or its objectives shall be punished by a term of imprisonment of between one and three years, and if the crime is committed through the press or other media, the sentence shall be increased by one half.

Article 314 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provides that anyone who forms an armed organisation to commit the crimes listed in the fourth and fifth sections of the relevant chapter, or commands such an organisation, shall be liable to a term of imprisonment of between ten and fifteen years.

Article 314 § 2 of the Turkish Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provides that anyone who becomes a member of an armed organisation mentioned in Article 314 § 1 shall be liable to a term of imprisonment of between five and ten years.

Article 314 § 3 of the Turkish Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provides that other provisions relating to the crime of establishing an organisation for the purpose of criminal activity are also applicable to the crime of membership of an armed organisation under Article 314.

At its 106th plenary session, held on 11 and 12 March 2016, the Venice Commission (European Commission for Democracy through Law) adopted an Opinion on Articles 216, 299, 301 and 314 of the Penal Code of Turkey (CDL-AD(2016)002).
In its Opinion CDL-AD(2016)002, the Venice Commission noted that the Turkish Penal Code does not contain a definition of an armed organisation or an armed group.

In its Opinion CDL-AD(2016)002, the Venice Commission noted that the Court of Cassation of Turkey developed the criterion of 'membership' in an armed organisation by examining different acts of the suspect, taking account of their 'continuity, diversity and intensity' in order to determine whether those acts prove an 'organic relationship' with the organisation or whether the acts may be considered as committed knowingly and wilfully within the 'hierarchical structure' of the organisation.

In its Opinion CDL-AD(2016)002, the Venice Commission noted that if an 'organic relationship' with the organisation cannot be proven on the basis of acts attributed to the defendant which do not present any 'continuity, diversity or intensity', the paragraphs on 'aiding and abetting an armed organisation' or 'committing crime on behalf of an armed organisation' under Article 220 of the Turkish Penal Code may be applied.

In its Opinion CDL-AD(2016)002, the Venice Commission noted that according to non-governmental sources, in the application of Article 314 of the Turkish Penal Code, domestic courts in many cases decide on the membership of a person in an armed organisation on the basis of very weak evidence, raising questions as to the 'foreseeability' of the application of Article 314.

In its Opinion CDL-AD(2016)002, the Venice Commission stated that conviction on the basis of weak evidence in the application of Article 314 of the Turkish Penal Code may create problems in the field of Article 7 of the Convention, since that provision embodies the principle that the criminal law must not be extensively construed to an accused's detriment, for instance by analogy.

In its Opinion CDL-AD(2016)002, the Venice Commission recommended that the sentence 'although he is not a member of that organisation, shall also be sentenced for the offence of being a member of that organisation' in paragraphs 6 and 7 of Article 220 of the Turkish Penal Code be repealed.

Mr Thomas Hammarberg stated in his report of 10 January 2012 that the provisions contained in the Turkish anti-terror legislation and Article 220 of the Turkish Criminal Code allow for a very wide margin of appreciation, in particular in cases where membership in a terrorist organisation has not been proven and when an act or statement may be deemed to coincide with the aims or instructions of a terrorist organisation.
Mr Nils Muižnieks, in his memorandum CommDH(2017)5 of 15 February 2017, stressed the need for a complete overhaul of the Turkish Criminal Code, including Article 220 §§ 6 and 7 and Article 314.

The Human Rights Watch report of 1 November 2010 stated that legal amendments since 2005, along with case law since 2008, have allowed courts in Turkey to convict demonstrators under the harshest terrorism laws, by invoking two articles of the Turkish Penal Code in combination with the Anti-Terror Law.

The Human Rights Watch report of 1 November 2010 stated that Turkish Penal Code Articles 220/6 and 220/7 are so vaguely worded and lacking in clarity about what is prohibited as to offer an individual no indication of how to regulate or limit conduct.

The Human Rights Watch report of 1 November 2010 recommended that the Turkish Government urgently amend Turkish Penal Code Article 220 and repeal Articles 220/6 and 220/7, which are vague, lack legal clarity and specificity, and are therefore subject to arbitrary application.
The applicants were taken into police custody on suspicion of aiding and abetting the MLKP (Marxist-Leninist Communist Party).
The MLKP (Marxist-Leninist Communist Party) was classified as an illegal armed organisation.
According to information on the Internet, the ESP (the Socialist Platform of the Oppressed) and the SGD (Socialist Youth Association) were connected to the MLKP (Marxist-Leninist Communist Party).

In its judgment, the Ankara Assize Court noted that although the ESP (Socialist Platform of the Oppressed) and the SGD (Socialist Youth Association) were legal entities, their activities were in line with those of the MLKP (Marxist-Leninist Communist Party).

The Ankara Assize Court considered that the ESP (Socialist Platform of the Oppressed) and the SGD (Socialist Youth Association) appeared in the legal domain on behalf of the MLKP (Marxist-Leninist Communist Party) and had an organic relationship with it.

The Ankara Assize Court found that the acts of Levent Çakır, Uğur Güdük, Latife Canan Kaplan, Serdar Kır, Selçuk Mart, Mehmet Ali Tosun, Filiz Uluçelebi and Mesut Açıkalın had constituted propaganda in favour of the MLKP (Marxist-Leninist Communist Party) and thereby propaganda inciting people to commit violence or other methods of terrorism.

In its Opinion CDL-AD(2016)002, the Venice Commission noted that in the case of Yılmaz and Kılıç v. Turkey (application no. 68514/01), the European Court of Human Rights considered that where the only evidence which led to the criminal conviction of the applicants under Article 169 of the former Turkish Penal Code was forms of expression (statements by the applicants, content of the slogans they shouted during a public demonstration), it should be concluded that there was an interference with the applicants' right to freedom of expression.

In its Opinion CDL-AD(2016)002, the Venice Commission noted that the European Court of Human Rights applied the same principle in the case of Gül and Others v. Turkey (application no. 4870/02) and held that the criminal conviction of the applicants on the basis of Article 169 of the former Turkish Penal Code constituted an interference with their right to freedom of expression, since the only evidence used against them was the content of the slogans they shouted during a public demonstration.

In its Opinion CDL-AD(2016)002, the Venice Commission stated that the expression of an opinion in its different forms should not be the only evidence before domestic courts to decide on the membership of a defendant in an armed organisation.

The Human Rights Watch report of 1 November 2010 stated that many hundreds of people in Turkey face prosecution, or are serving substantial sentences for terrorism convictions, where their 'crime' was to engage in peaceful protest, or to throw stones or burn a tire at a protest.

The Amnesty International report of 27 March 2013 stated that Article 220/7 of the Turkish Penal Code is often used to prosecute conduct protected by the rights to freedom of expression, association and assembly.

The Amnesty International report of 27 March 2013 stated that no inference should be drawn from someone undertaking a lawful act, such as participating in a peaceful demonstration, even if such acts benefit, through lawful means, goals shared by a terrorist organisation.
